title: Letting the story change
hook: the story of the hurt can change as you do

segments.voice: Yesterday, reconciling, and the sage who keeps the tally without collecting. Your line was when it's safe. Today, something you can change even when no one else is willing: the way you tell it.

Every hurt comes with a story, and the story gets told. To a friend the week it happens, hot and fast. To a partner a year later, with a sigh. To yourself in the car, in the same words every time, like a song on repeat. The facts in those stories don't change; what happened, happened. But the telling can change, because the teller does. The book of Ruth has a woman whose story is told one way in its first chapter and another way in its last. Today: letting the story change.
screen: `EVERY HURT HAS A STORY.` → `THE FACTS STAY.` → `THE TELLER CHANGES.`

segments.voice: First, the first telling. Naomi has buried her husband and both her sons in a foreign country. When she comes home to Bethlehem, the women of the town ask, is this Naomi? She answers, in the King James words: "Call me not Naomi, call me Mara: for the Almighty hath dealt very bitterly with me." Naomi means pleasant. Mara means bitter. She renames herself after the hurt. Second, that telling was true. She goes on: "I went out full, and the LORD hath brought me home again empty." The book doesn't correct her. Nobody tells her to look on the bright side. The bitter telling gets its full say, and it stays in the book. Third, the second telling. By the last chapter a lot has happened: Ruth's loyalty, a harvest, a marriage, a baby. And the women of the town tell the story again: "There is a son born to Naomi." Naomi, not Mara. The graves from chapter one are still there. What changed is that the story kept going, and so did she. Fourth, a test for a new telling. Is it still true? Does it still name the loss, or the wrong, plainly? And does it have room for who you are now, not only who you were the day it happened? A new telling isn't a happier lie. It's the same facts, told by someone who has kept living.
screen: `CALL ME MARA.` · `I WENT OUT FULL.` · `A SON BORN TO NAOMI.` · `THE SAME FACTS, A LIVING TELLER.` · then, large: `A NEW TELLING.`

segments.voice: Choose one hurt you've told many times, and hear the usual telling once, in its usual words. Now tell it again silently, keeping the facts exactly and naming the wrong plainly, but add one sentence about what came after, something you did, learned or survived; if there's no after yet, the sentence can be: and I'm still here. Let the new telling sit without forcing a happy ending, and if you pray, you can offer both versions in your prayer.
Mara. The name Naomi gave herself after her losses, bitter, before the story was told again at the book's end. Today's word.
Your line: a new telling. Naomi's story didn't stop at Mara. That's day nine hundred ninety-one.

chat.says: Every time I tell the story of that breakup, I feel worse. Should I stop telling it?
options: Try a new telling: same facts, the wrong named, plus what came after.
Tell a happier version, even if it means leaving the hard parts out.
Keep telling it the same way; changing it would mean it wasn't true.
chat.meaning: Naomi's bitter telling stays true in Ruth, and the story still gets told again. A new telling keeps the facts and has room for who you are now.
